tldr:
Before a tool set ships, **measure** whether the model picks the right tool **with the right input**. The guide's instruction (§7): **test tool-selection reliability with ambiguous requests**. The method comes from the docs:

- A test set that mirrors real traffic, including **ambiguous and edge cases**.
- **Specific, measurable bars per category**, not one average.
- **Automated exact grading**: the right job and the right input.
- **Re-run everything after every change.**

When a category fails, the fix the docs and guide point to is **sharper tool descriptions**, not a bigger model.
mentalModel: An eval is a driving test with the hard junctions on the route. A test that only has straight roads (clear requests) passes a driver who can't handle a roundabout (ambiguous requests). One overall score hides the roundabout. And after a repair you re-drive the whole route, not just the corner that failed last time.
whatItIs:
The exam guide has **no task statement on evaluation**. Its study advice says to test tool selection with ambiguous requests
(Guide §7 · How to Prepare · p.24). Task statement 2.1 (p.9) explains why it matters: minimal or overlapping descriptions make
selection unreliable. The **method** on this page comes from the platform docs (*Define success and build evaluations*,
*Troubleshooting tool use*).

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ambiguous test cases | Put the roundabout on the test route, or you'll never see the driver fail it. | ⭐ Guide §7 · p.24; TS 2.1 · Knowledge 3 |
| 2 | Per-category success criteria | A report card with a mark per subject — an average hides the failed one. | 📘 docs |
| 3 | Specific, measurable bars | “Ambiguous ≥ 90%” can fail; “works well” can't. | 📘 docs |
| 4 | Exact, automated grading | Check the answer against the key, not whether the student wrote something. | 📘 docs |
| 5 | Grade the input too | The right tool with the wrong order id still sends the customer the wrong parcel. | 📘 docs |
| 6 | Full re-run after a change | Re-drive the whole route after a repair — the fix can break another corner. | 💡 my recommendation (docs principle) |
| 7 | Fix = sharper descriptions | When the tool choice fails, rewrite WHEN to use each tool, not the test. | ⭐ TS 2.1 · Knowledge 1, Skill 1; 📘 docs |

**Grading methods** (docs)

| # | Method | Good for | In this lab |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Exact match (code) | Categorical answers with one right value | ✅ The tool's job, and the order id |
| 2 | String match (code) | Output that must contain a phrase | — |
| 3 | LLM-based grading | Nuance: tone, empathy (use a **different** model to grade) | — |
| 4 | Human grading | Small, hard sets | — (the docs prefer more automated cases) |

**What a good tool-selection eval looks like**

| # | Part | This lab |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Clear requests | 10 — one right tool each |
| 2 | ⭐ Ambiguous requests | 3 — web search results that sound like documents |
| 3 | Edge cases | 3 — bare order numbers that must be formatted `ORD-####` |
| 4 | Bars | clear 95% · ambiguous 90% · edge 100% |
| 5 | Grader | exact job + exact input |
| 6 | After a change | the whole suite again |
howItWorks:
1. **Collect requests that mirror real traffic,** including ambiguous and edge cases, each labelled with the right job
   (and input).
2. **Set a bar per category** — specific and measurable.
3. **Grade automatically and exactly:** the job the chosen tool does, and its input where it matters.
4. **Report per category and decide:** ship only if every category meets its bar.
5. **When a category fails,** sharpen the descriptions (say WHEN to use each tool; add boundaries). Then re-run the
   **whole** suite.
whereSeen:
- **Scenario 1 — Customer Support Resolution Agent** (Guide §5, p.3): tools with overlapping purposes that must be told apart.
- **Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System** (Guide §5, p.4): web results vs documents — the ambiguity this lab tests.
- **Guide §8, Exercise 1** (pp.24–25): build tools with similar functionality and test that the agent picks correctly.

grounding.text: Good success criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant; most use cases need several criteria (multidimensional evaluation), not one number.
Evals should mirror the real task distribution and include edge cases — including ambiguous cases where even humans would disagree.
grounding.ref: develop-tests § Eval design principles; edge cases

grounding.text: Automate grading where possible (exact match, string match, code-graded, LLM-graded); more automated questions beat fewer hand-graded ones.
Exact-match evaluation suits categorical answers with a clear correct value.
When LLM-based grading is used, grade with a different model from the one that produced the output.
Claude calls tool A instead of B → sharpen descriptions, differentiating tools by WHEN to use them; wrong parameter types → strict: true or input_examples.

grounding.text: Preparation advice: test tool-selection reliability with ambiguous requests, alongside descriptions that clearly differentiate similar tools.

Tool descriptions are the main way the model selects tools; minimal ones make selection among similar tools unreliable, and ambiguous or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting (analyze_content vs analyze_document).
The guide has no task statement on evaluation; the evaluation method on this page comes from the platform docs.
Re-running the whole suite after every change (not just the cases that failed before) is this page's recommendation, following the docs' 'mirror the real task distribution' principle.
The router, the tool-set versions, the production traffic and the 90 % bar that judges a release are invented.

labIntro:
You write an **eval harness**: a test set, success criteria, a grader, a release decision and a re-run policy. The lab runs it
on a candidate tool set through the **simulated** tool router from D2.1. It then shows what that tool set does on
**production traffic you never saw**. The question every time: **did your harness make the right call?**

- **v1:** a vague web tool.
- **v2:** sharpened descriptions.
- **v3:** v2, but the order-id formatting rule was lost.

labScenarios.title: A vague web tool
labScenarios.description: Candidate v1 describes its web tool as just “Analyzes content.” — will your eval catch that web-results requests misroute?

labScenarios.title: Sharpened descriptions
labScenarios.description: Candidate v2 is good in every category — your eval should let it ship.

labScenarios.title: A fix that breaks something else
labScenarios.description: v3 fixes v1's web-results problem but lost the ORD-#### formatting rule for order ids.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ ambiguous cases in the suite · per-category bars · exact grading · full re-run
variants.code:
from utils.eval_lab import job, release     # SIMULATED tool router + release gate

C = lambda request, expect, category, expect_input=None: {
    "request": request, "expect": expect, "category": category, "expect_input": expect_input}

# 1. A test set that mirrors real traffic: clear requests, AMBIGUOUS ones and edge cases
TEST_SET = [
    C("Does the attached report actually support the claim that churn fell 5%?", "verify", "clear"),
    C("Does the attached audit actually support the claim that prices rose 8%?", "verify", "clear"),
    C("Extract every price and date from the uploaded contract PDF.", "extract", "clear"),
    C("Pull the payment terms and amounts out of the attached invoice PDF.", "extract", "clear"),
    C("Where is the order for carol@example.com?", "customer", "clear"),
    C("Find the customer record for erin@example.com.", "customer", "clear"),
    C("Give me a short summary of the attached quarterly report.", "summarize", "clear"),
    C("Condense the attached annual report into a short overview.", "summarize", "clear"),
    C("Does the attached report actually support the claim that sales doubled?", "verify", "clear"),
    C("Extract all names and dates from the attached PDF agreement.", "extract", "clear"),
    C("Pull the key facts out of these web search results about solar panel prices.", "web", "ambiguous"),
    C("Turn these web search results into a short summary for the team.", "web", "ambiguous"),
    C("Summarize the key facts from these web results on heat pumps.", "web", "ambiguous"),
    C("What's the status of order 1001?", "order", "edge", {"order_id": "ORD-1001"}),
    C("order 2002 - has it shipped?", "order", "edge", {"order_id": "ORD-2002"}),
    C("Has order 5005 arrived yet?", "order", "edge", {"order_id": "ORD-5005"}),
]

# 2. Specific, measurable criteria - one per category, not one overall number
CRITERIA = {"clear": 0.95, "ambiguous": 0.90, "edge": 1.00}


def grade(case, result):
    """Code-based exact match: the right JOB, and the right INPUT where it matters."""
    if job(result["tool"]) != case["expect"]:
        return False
    return case["expect_input"] is None or result["input"] == case["expect_input"]


def decide(report):
    """Ship only if EVERY category meets its bar."""
    for category, bar in CRITERIA.items():
        if category not in report:
            print(f"no test cases for '{category}' - can't claim it works")
            return False
        if report[category]["accuracy"] < bar:
            print(f"'{category}' at {report[category]['accuracy']:.0%} is below its bar of {bar:.0%}")
            return False
    return True


def select_cases(test_set, previous_failures):
    """After a change, re-run the WHOLE suite - a fix in one place can break another."""
    return test_set


release(TEST_SET, grade, decide, select_cases)
variants.observe: ambiguous_traffic: clear 10/10, edge 3/3, but ambiguous 0/3 — every web-results request goes to a document tool (extract_data_points / summarize_content). “'ambiguous' at 0% is below its bar of 90%” → BLOCK, and production agrees (ambiguous 0.0). fixed_tools: 16/16 → SHIP, production all 1.0. regression: v3 fixed the web requests but order ids come back as '1001' not 'ORD-1001' → edge 0/3 → BLOCK.
variants.why: The suite looks like real traffic (including the ambiguous requests the guide says to test), every category has its own measurable bar, the grader checks the exact job AND input, and the whole suite runs after every change.

distractors.name: A · No ambiguous test cases

distractors.instead: Ambiguous + edge cases with their own bar.

distractors.fails: A 0% category hides inside the average.

distractors.name: C · “Any tool call” passes
distractors.looks: The agent did call a tool.

distractors.fails: Stale results hide the new breakage.

experiments: Run ✅ on all three scenarios and read the per-category report next to production.
In ✅, delete the three ambiguous cases and run ambiguous_traffic — that's ❌ A.
In ✅, lower the ambiguous bar to 0.0: what does the harness decide for v1?
Run ❌ D on regression and find the “reused 13 results” line.
Type your own request in the playground's “Try a request” tab; if v1 and v2 disagree, it belongs in the suite.

questions.q: A team's tool-selection eval scores 100% on 200 requests, yet in production the agent routes about 1 in 5 questions about web search results to the document-analysis tool. All 200 eval requests are clear-cut, such as “search the web for…” or “analyse this PDF…”. What should change first?
opts: Add ambiguous requests that could plausibly fit either tool, since that is where misrouting happens.
Double the eval set to 400 clear-cut requests, so that the headline score is statistically more reliable.
Raise the ship threshold from 95% to 99%, so that only near-perfect tool selection can be released.
Replace the eval with production sampling, since offline evals can't predict production behaviour.
questions.explain: Misrouting happens where tool descriptions overlap, on ambiguous requests. An eval with none of those cannot see it. B adds more of the easy cases. C raises the bar on a test that can't fail. D abandons pre-release testing instead of fixing its coverage.

questions.q: A support agent's eval shows it picks get_customer instead of lookup_order on 48% of requests that mention both a customer name and an order number. The two descriptions are “Retrieves customer information” and “Retrieves order details”. Which fix addresses the root cause?
opts: Change the eval so either tool counts as correct, since both can eventually lead to the right order.
Add a keyword router that sends any request containing an order number straight to lookup_order.
Rewrite both descriptions to state what each accepts and when to use it rather than the other.
Add 10 few-shot examples of mixed requests to the system prompt, each one routed to lookup_order.
questions.explain: The eval found the symptom, and the minimal descriptions are the cause. Descriptions that give inputs and boundaries fix it. A hides the failure by redefining success. B bypasses the model's selection with a brittle layer. D adds tokens but leaves the descriptions ambiguous.

questions.q: An eval reports: clear requests 100%, ambiguous requests 0%, edge cases 100%, which averages to 81% overall. The release rule is “ship if overall ≥ 80%”, so the build shipped, and ambiguous production requests immediately started failing. What is wrong with this gate?
opts: The 80% threshold is too low; raising it to 90% would have blocked this particular release.
An overall average hides a segment that fails completely; gate on each segment's criterion too.
The ambiguous segment is too small to matter, so it should be removed from the eval instead.
The eval should weight edge cases more heavily, since they are the hardest requests to get right.
questions.explain: A single average can pass while a whole segment fails, so each segment needs its own success criterion. A might block this release, but any average can hide a failing segment. C and D change the maths instead of looking at the failure.

questions.q: After a description change fixes 14 misrouted requests, a developer re-runs only those 14 cases, sees them pass, and ships. A week later, 9 requests that used to be routed correctly start failing. What should the process have been?
opts: Add the 9 new failures to the targeted set, and re-run only the failing cases after the next change.
Ship description changes behind a feature flag, and roll back whenever production errors appear.
Freeze tool descriptions after launch, since every change risks breaking requests that already work.
Re-run the whole eval suite after every change, so regressions are caught before release.
questions.explain: A description change can shift routing anywhere, so the full suite is the regression check. A repeats the same blind spot. B finds regressions in production. D stops improvement altogether.

faq.q: Is tool evaluation on the exam?
faq.a: The guide has no task statement for it. Its study advice (§7, p.24) says to test tool selection with ambiguous requests. TS 2.1 covers why selection fails. Questions tend to ask about the fix — sharper descriptions — rather than eval design.

faq.q: Why grade the input and not just the tool?
faq.a: A call to the right tool with a wrong argument (1001 instead of ORD-1001) still fails. The docs treat wrong parameters as a failure of their own, fixed with strict: true or input_examples.

faq.q: Should an LLM grade tool selection?
faq.a: Not usually — the right tool is a categorical answer, so exact matching in code is simpler and more reliable. The docs keep LLM grading for nuance like tone, and say to grade with a different model.

faq.q: How big should the suite be?
faq.a: The docs favour more automated cases over fewer hand-graded ones. Make every category big enough that its bar means something.

playgroundIntro:
Switch the harness's choices on and off and pick a candidate tool set. Each run shows your per-category report, your ship or
block decision, and the production truth. The last tab routes any request you type through the vague and the sharpened tool
sets. If they disagree, that request belongs in your test set.

playground.label: ⭐ Test-set coverage
playground.mentalModel: Put the roundabout on the route.
playground.meaning: Does the suite contain ambiguous requests?
tryThis: v1 without them: SHIP a bad release.

playground.label: Success criteria
playground.mentalModel: A mark per subject, not an average.
playground.meaning: 📘 Per-category bars vs one overall number.
tryThis: overall ≥ 80% on v1: SHIP at 81% with ambiguous 0%.
overall ≥ 80% on v3: SHIP with edge 0%.

playground.label: Grader
playground.mentalModel: Check the answer against the key.
playground.meaning: 📘 Exact grading of job + input, job only, or “a tool was called”.
tryThis: any tool on v1: 16/16, SHIP a bad release.
job only on v3: misses the '1001' ids.
job only on v1: still blocks (the jobs are wrong).

playground.label: Re-run after a change
playground.mentalModel: Re-drive the whole route after a repair.
playground.meaning: 💡 v3 fixed v1's failures: re-run everything, or only what failed last time?
tryThis: failures only: 3 cases re-run, 13 stale results reused → SHIP a bad release.

playground.label: Try a request
playground.mentalModel: If the two tool sets disagree, the request belongs in the suite.
playground.meaning: Route any request through v1 (vague web tool) and v2 (sharpened).
